subject: Civil Engineering
title: Rigid Pavements: Concrete Roads
description: Learn Rigid Pavements: Concrete Roads in one minute.

hook.text: An interstate through the Midwest uses concrete slabs — bumpy joints every 15 feet.

buildup.text: Rigid pavements use thick concrete slabs. The slab itself spreads the load over a wide area.

discovery.text: Joints prevent random cracking — saw-cut lines tell the concrete where to crack neatly.

twist.text: Dowel bars cross the joints — they transfer load between slabs while allowing expansion.

climax.text: Continuously reinforced concrete has no joints — steel holds the cracks tight.

punchline.text: Concrete roads last longer but cost more. The trade-off defines every project.

quiz.question: Why are joints cut into concrete pavement slabs?
options: To make the road more flexible under heavy traffic
To control where cracks form so they occur in neat, planned lines
To allow water to drain through the pavement surface

details.summary: Rigid pavements use Portland cement concrete slabs that distribute traffic loads across large areas through the slab's bending stiffness. Joints are placed at regular intervals to control cracking from thermal expansion, and dowel bars transfer loads between adjacent slabs to prevent faulting.
details.whyItMatters: Concrete pavements last 30-50 years with minimal maintenance, making them cost-effective for heavy-traffic roads. They perform better than asphalt under extreme heat and heavy truck loads.
takeaways: Concrete slabs distribute loads through bending stiffness, not layer thickness
Transverse joints every 4-6 meters control random cracking from shrinkage
Dowel bars across joints transfer loads and prevent step-offs between slabs

faq.question: Why do concrete pavements need joints?
faq.answer: Concrete shrinks as it cures and expands and contracts with temperature changes. Without joints, these stresses would cause random uncontrolled cracks. Joints create planned weak points where controlled cracks form in straight lines that can be sealed against water infiltration.

faq.question: What is continuously reinforced concrete pavement?
faq.answer: CRCP uses continuous steel reinforcement to hold tight transverse cracks together instead of using joints. Cracks form naturally every one to two meters but are held so tightly by the steel that they seal themselves and transfer loads effectively. CRCP eliminates joint maintenance entirely.
